title: 4 Maccabees
subtitle: godly reason on trial: an old priest, seven brothers and their mother before the tyrant
lead: 4 Maccabees is not a history but a speech. Its speaker sets out to prove one claim, "whether godly reason is master in its own right over the passions" (1:1): whether a mind trained by God's law can rule fear, pain, desire and even a mother's love. He proves it first from the law of Moses and from Joseph, Moses, Jacob and David (1:1-3:18). Then he proves it at length from the martyrs whose deaths 2 Maccabees tells in a chapter and a half (2 Maccabees 6:18-7:42): the old priest Eleazar, seven brothers and their mother, tortured to death by the Greek king Antiochus IV for refusing to eat pork (3:19-17:6). He ends with their reward, their meaning for the nation, and the mother's last words to her sons (17:7-18:24). It has 18 chapters and 484 verses.

Who reads it as Scripture. No church source opened for this page counts 4 Maccabees among its canonical books. The preface to the NRSV Apocrypha says that "4 Maccabees appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible," and an Orthodox priest and scholar, Fr. Stephen De Young, calls it "a Biblical text that lies at the very edges of the Old Testament canon in the Orthodox Church." The old lists of the books do not agree. The Apostolic Canons count "of the Maccabees, three" without naming them; the Stichometry of Nicephorus counts three books of Maccabees among the disputed books; a Synopsis of Scripture ascribed to Athanasius counts four among the books outside its list; and the Latin list in Codex Claromontanus names a first, a second and a fourth book (Swete). It is not in the Catholic, Protestant, Ethiopian or Jewish Bible, it was never in the Latin Vulgate, and a Coptic Orthodox diocese says it is not in that church's canon. Yet the Orthodox Church keeps the martyrs it praises as saints on 1 August (OCA), the West once honored them too (Townshend), and early Christian preachers knew the book well. Scholars date it between the first century BC and the end of the first century AD (Townshend; Swete; De Young) and read it as the work of a Greek-speaking Jew, a window on how Jews of the Diaspora joined Greek philosophy to the law of Moses, and on how they spoke of martyrs whose death could cleanse the nation (6:28-29; 17:20-22).
facts: No church source opened for this page holds it as canonical. "4 Maccabees appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible" (NRSV preface); later Greek manuscripts put it in an appendix, and it is in Old Georgian Old Testaments and was for a time in the Romanian (De Young). Not in the Russian Synodal Bible, whose list of books (azbyka.ru) has three books of Maccabees, each marked non-canonical. Not canonical for the Coptic Orthodox Church (a diocese's answer). Not in the Bible of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Not Scripture for the Catholic Church, Protestants or Judaism.

Unknown: a Greek-speaking Jew trained in Greek rhetoric and philosophy. Eusebius and Jerome credited it to Josephus, and it was long printed among his works; scholars reject this (Townshend; the Catholic Encyclopedia).

Debated, between the first century BC and the end of the first century AD: between 63 BC and AD 38 (Townshend); "during the century before the fall of Jerusalem" (Swete); before the fall of Jerusalem (the Catholic Encyclopedia, Reid); the end of the first century AD (De Young).
Jerusalem under the Seleucid kings Seleucus IV and Antiochus IV, about 175-167 BC: the Temple treasury, the high priests Onias and Jason, and the persecution.
Debated: Alexandria (Townshend, Swete) or Antioch in Syria (De Young).
Greek, in ornate, "truly Greek" rhetoric (Swete), with words the writer coined himself, such as autodespotos, "master in its own right" (1:1; Townshend). It was never in Hebrew.

Greek, in three great codices: Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD); not in Vaticanus. Also in manuscripts of Josephus's works and in a Syriac version (Townshend).

A philosophical speech (logos, 1:1) joined to a speech of praise for martyrs: a thesis and definitions (1:1-30), proofs from the law (1:31-3:18), and the martyrs as proof (3:19-18:24), with speeches, prayers, an imagined epitaph (17:9-10) and the mother's speech to her sons (18:6-19).
18 chapters, 484 verses, in the numbering of Swete's Greek, which the site follows. Brenton's English of 1851 numbers chapters 7, 8, 10 and 11 differently.
authorship: The early church credited the book to Josephus, the Jewish historian. Eusebius says the same writer produced "another work of no little merit," "On the Supremacy of Reason, which some have called Maccabaicum, because it contains an account of the struggles of those Hebrews who contended manfully for the true religion" (Church History 3.10.6). Jerome calls it a book of his "in which the martyr deaths of the Maccabeans are related" and says it "is highly esteemed" (Lives of Illustrious Men 13). So it was copied and printed among Josephus's works, under titles such as "Josippus on the Maccabees" (Townshend; Swete).

Not Josephus. Townshend (1913) gave the reasons: the book calls Antiochus IV the son of Seleucus IV (4:15), where Josephus rightly calls him his brother; it has Antiochus win all his wars by the martyrs' example (17:23-24), where Josephus tells of his failure at Elymais; its speaker and hearers live in peace and safety (14:9), which does not fit the man who saw Jerusalem fall; it keeps the Hebrew forms of names that Josephus turns into Greek; and its style and its ideal, to die rather than give way, are far from his. The Catholic Encyclopedia (Reid) says it "was erroneously ascribed to Josephus by Eusebius and others."
What can be known of the author

He was a Jew loyal to the law of Moses who wrote Greek as his own language and knew the Greek schools well (Townshend; Swete). He calls his work a "most philosophical" speech (1:1), addresses his hearers as "you" and speaks of his own habit of first setting out his subject (1:12). Ewald suggested that his real name was Josephus, which would explain the confusion with the historian; Townshend thought this possible but of little use.

According to Townshend, some commentators have thought that the book first ended at 18:2, so that the mother's account of her life (18:6-19), which comes after the story has ended (18:5), would be a later addition. Townshend answers that it is a digression the writer meant, a praise of the mother's virtues at home, and sees "no reason why we should look in this last chapter for traces of another hand." All three codices have it.

audience.to: Greek-speaking Jews of a large city of the Diaspora in the first century AD, people at home in Greek schools, Greek games and Greek philosophy, who heard their neighbors call the law of Moses irrational and their food laws absurd (5:7-11). The speaker addresses them as "you" (1:1; 3:2-4) and speaks of them as living in safety: "Now, we shudder just hearing about what those young men went through" (14:9). Which city is debated: Alexandria (Townshend; Swete) or Antioch, where the martyrs' shrine stood, first Jewish and later Christian (De Young).
audience.why: To prove to people who admired Greek thought that the law of Moses is the true philosophy (5:22-24), that the virtues the Greeks praise are reached best by a mind trained in that law (1:17-18; 2:21-23), and so to make them ready to keep it even to death, as Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother did. The speaker answers a pressure his hearers felt: to treat the law as one custom among many, to eat as others ate, to fit in. He says that keeping it is not stubbornness but reason, and that those who died for it "live to God" (7:19; 16:25). Knowing the audience changes the reading: the tortures are not told for their own sake but as a demonstration, aimed at hearers who had to choose every day how Jewish to be in a Greek city.
views: The speaker praises those who died "at this season" (1:10), which can be read as the time of a yearly remembrance. Freudenthal, with whom Ewald seems to agree, took the book as an example of synagogue preaching. Other commentators answer that a synagogue sermon in the Diaspora took a passage of the Bible as its text, and this speech does not, so it was more likely a lecture. Townshend adds that "the best authorities doubt" whether enough is known of the practice of the time to decide (Townshend).

Townshend thought the most likely reason was the worship of the Roman emperors: a far-sighted Jew could foresee that one day Jews would be told to sacrifice at the emperor's altars, and wrote to prepare them; the crisis came in Alexandria in AD 38-39 under Caligula.
A book for the martyrs' city

De Young links the writing of the book to "the prominence of the martyrs in the Jewish community of Antioch in the first century," where their relics were kept in a shrine, "first Jewish and later Christian," and says that before they were Christian saints they were remembered in synagogues with a fast on the 9th of Av.

outline: The thesis: godly reason is master over the passions; the plan of the speech
Definitions: reason, wisdom, the four virtues, the passions and their two roots, pleasure and pain
Reason and the law: food laws, Joseph, the tenth commandment, money, enemies; God gave the mind and the law together
Reason does not uproot the passions but fights them: Jacob on Simeon and Levi; David's thirst
The history: peace under the law; Simon, Onias and Apollonius at the Temple treasury
Antiochus IV, Jason's high priesthood and gymnasium, the decree against the law
Eleazar before Antiochus: the king's speech that the law is against nature, and Eleazar's answer that it is reason's own philosophy
Eleazar's torture and death; his prayer that his blood cleanse the people (6:27-29)
The first conclusion and the praise of Eleazar
The seven brothers before the king: his offer, the instruments of torture, the cowardly speech they did not make
The deaths of the seven brothers, one by one; the youngest throws himself into the fire
The brothers' courage and their love for each other
The mother: love of children, her choice, the comparison with Abraham, her words to her sons
The mother's death; the epitaph the speaker would write on their tomb
The divine contest and its prize; what the martyrs' death did for the nation; the tyrant's punishment
The mother's speech to her sons: her life, their father's teaching, the heroes and the Scriptures
The bitter day, the tyrant's end, and the closing praise

lenses.name: Orthodox
lenses.desc: The NRSV preface says that "4 Maccabees appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible," and an Orthodox priest and scholar places it "at the very edges of the Old Testament canon in the Orthodox Church" (De Young); the martyrs it praises are Orthodox saints, kept on 1 August (OCA). The lens reads the book as Orthodox readers meet it: a witness to the martyrs, and a link between the wisdom books and the church's later teaching on the passions and the virtues.

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Most scholars read 4 Maccabees as a speech by a Greek-speaking Jew of the first century AD, which retells 2 Maccabees 6-7 freely to prove a philosophical thesis, and they ask when, where and for whom it was written and how its history differs from 2 Maccabees.

lenses.name: Jewish reception
lenses.desc: 4 Maccabees is not in the Jewish Bible and had little influence on later Judaism (Townshend), but the rabbis told their own story of a mother and seven sons (Bavli Gittin 57b), and the book shows how Greek-speaking Jews before the rabbis read the law, the martyrs and the life to come.

lenses.name: New Testament background
lenses.desc: Readers who study the world of the first Christians: martyrs whose blood could cleanse a nation and be "a life in exchange" (6:29; 17:22), endurance in a contest watched by the world (17:11-16), faith in God and those who "live to God" (7:19; 16:25), set beside Hebrews 11-12, Paul's use of hilastērion (Romans 3:25) and the Gospels, with how strong or weak each link is.

lenses.name: Greek philosophy
lenses.desc: Readers who trace the book's Greek ideas: Stoic and Platonic teaching on reason, the passions and the four virtues of good sense, justice, courage and self-restraint (1:18), and how far the book bends them to the law of Moses, for example by holding that reason rules the passions but does not uproot them (3:5).

lenses.name: Western churches: read, not Scripture
lenses.desc: Catholic and Protestant readers: a Jewish writing that was never in the Latin Vulgate or in their Apocrypha, read for its witness to Jewish faith before Christ and to the martyrs both churches honored, and tested against the Bible rather than read as the Bible.

sections.b:
Read it as a speech with a thesis, not as a story told for its own sake. The speaker states his question in the first verse, "whether godly reason is master in its own right over the passions" (1:1), and tells you his plan: he could prove it from many examples, but best from those who died for virtue, Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother (1:7-9). He will praise their virtues and call them blessed for their honors (1:10). Every scene that follows is a proof of that claim, and he keeps saying so (6:31-35; 7:16-23; 13:1-5; 16:1-4; 18:2).

Read it in three movements. First, the argument: what reason, wisdom and the passions are (1:13-30), and how the law trains the mind to rule hunger, desire, greed and anger, with Joseph, Moses, Jacob and David as examples (1:31-3:18). Second, the history that led to the persecution (3:19-4:26). Third, the martyrs, told at length and with the speaker's own comments between the scenes (5:1-18:24).

Expect the tortures to be told plainly and in detail. Townshend (1913) noted that this "shocks modern taste" but reminded readers that the first hearers lived where torture was public. The detail serves the argument: the worse the pain, the stronger the reason that ruled it. Notice too what the book leaves out: there is no Judas Maccabeus and no armed revolt. Its heroes win by enduring, and the speaker says their endurance cleansed the homeland (1:11; 17:21).

The martyrs are not the Maccabees in the strict sense: Judas Maccabeus and his brothers led the revolt of 1 and 2 Maccabees, and this book never names them. The name came from the books of Maccabees, whose martyrs it retells. The Catholic Encyclopedia (Bechtel) puts it simply: the fourth book has the name "because it speaks of the Machabee martyrs." In the great codices it is Makkabaiōn d', "Of the Maccabees, fourth" (Townshend; Swete). Christians in time called the martyrs themselves "the Holy Maccabees."

The older title describes its subject. Eusebius calls it On the Supremacy of Reason (Peri autokratoros logismou), "which some have called Maccabaicum" (Church History 3.10.6), and Jerome knew it by the same Greek title (Lives of Illustrious Men 13).

The writer calls his work a logos, a speech or discourse (1:1). Townshend calls it "a discourse or treatise," and De Young a philosophical treatise that "also has features of a homily or oration." It quotes the tenth commandment (2:5) and uses the heroes of the Bible as examples, but it does not take one passage of Scripture as its text and expound it. For that reason other commentators, Townshend says, judged it a lecture rather than a synagogue sermon, against Freudenthal and Ewald, who took it as a sermon; Townshend thought the evidence too thin to decide.

Its Greek is the most literary in the Greek Bible. Swete calls the style "truly Greek," nearer than any other book of the Greek Bible "to the models of Hellenic philosophy and rhetoric," though full of "false ornament and laboured periods." Townshend lists words the writer seems to have coined: autodespotos, "master in its own right" (1:1), heptamētōr, "mother of seven" (16:24), and pēdaliouchein, "to steer," used of reason as the pilot of godliness (7:1). The Plain English Translation breaks the long periods into short sentences but keeps each clause.

The writer borrows the Greek schools' words and fills them with the law of Moses. Reason (logismos) is the mind choosing the life of wisdom (1:15). Wisdom is the knowledge of divine and human things and their causes, and this is "the training the law gives" (1:16-17). Its forms are the four virtues: good sense, justice, courage and self-restraint (1:18), the same four Greek words that Wisdom of Solomon 8:7 uses, though the Plain English Translation of Wisdom renders them differently ("self-control and understanding, righteousness and courage"). The Catholic Encyclopedia (Reid) says it was "through Fourth Machabees that this category was appropriated by early Christian ascetical writers."

He takes a Stoic thesis, that reason can master the passions, but he changes it in two ways. First, the reason that rules is godly reason, a mind trained by God's law (1:1; 1:17). When Eleazar lists what "our philosophy" teaches, he adds a fifth to the four virtues, godliness, "so that we worship with fitting honor only the God who truly is" (5:22-24; Townshend calls this "the key-note of his whole book"). Second, the Stoics held that the passions should be uprooted. This writer says God planted them in us when he made us, set the mind on its throne over them, and gave it the law (2:21-23): "Reason," in Townshend's translation of 3:5, "is not the extirpator of the passions, but their antagonist." He also takes the Stoic view that every sin is equally a breaking of the law (5:20; Townshend).

Townshend compared him to Philo of Alexandria, who used Greek philosophy as "a means of defending and justifying Jewish religious truths" (quoting the Jewish Encyclopedia). Fr. Stephen De Young sees "clear and direct lines of continuity" between the book's teaching on passions, desires and virtues and later Orthodox monastic writing.

Chapters 3-18 retell 2 Maccabees 3-7, and the differences are part of the book's message. Set the two side by side:

  • The Temple treasury. In 2 Maccabees 3 the king sends his minister Heliodorus, after Simon has gone to Apollonius, "governor of Coele-Syria and Phoenicia" (2 Maccabees 3:5). Here Apollonius, governor of "Syria, Phoenicia and Cilicia", goes himself, and angels on horseback stop him (4:2-10).
  • The king. Here Antiochus IV is the "son" of Seleucus IV (4:15); Townshend notes that Josephus rightly makes him his brother.
  • Jason's price. In 2 Maccabees, Jason promises "three hundred sixty talents of silver, plus eighty talents" and more for a gymnasium (2 Maccabees 4:8-9). Here he promises 3,660 talents a year (4:17), and builds the gymnasium "on top of our homeland's citadel" (4:20).
  • Eleazar. In 2 Maccabees he is "one of the foremost scribes" (2 Maccabees 6:18). Here he is a priest by family and an expert in the law (5:4), and the speech gives him long debates with the king (5:5-38).
  • The tortures. Told with "an even greater wealth of dreadful detail" than in 2 Maccabees (Townshend): the wheel, the catapult, the pans (8:13).
  • The mother's death. 2 Maccabees only says, "After her sons, last of all, the mother met her end" (2 Maccabees 7:41). Here, as some of the spearmen said, she threw herself into the fire so that no one would touch her body (17:1).
  • The hope. In 2 Maccabees the brothers hope for the raising of the body: "But the King of the world will raise us, who died for his laws, to live again forever" (2 Maccabees 7:9). Here they receive from God "souls that are pure and immortal" (18:23), and, in Townshend's words, "apparently there is no resurrection of the body."
  • The outcome. Here the martyrs' endurance so impresses Antiochus that he holds it up to his soldiers and wins all his wars (17:23-24), and after his failure in Jerusalem he marches against the Persians (18:5).

Whether the writer used 2 Maccabees itself or the longer history of Jason of Cyrene behind it, Townshend left open; Swete thought this part of the book "based on" 2 Maccabees 6:18-7:42.

sections.h: The martyrs' death and the New Testament
sections.b:
Two passages make 4 Maccabees one of the most discussed books for the background of the New Testament. Eleazar prays as he dies: "Be merciful to your nation. Let the penalty we pay on their account be enough for you. Make my blood their cleansing, and take my soul as a life in exchange for them" (6:28-29). Near the end the speaker says that the martyrs became "a life in exchange for the nation's sin," and: "Through the blood of those godly people and their atoning death, divine providence saved Israel" (17:21-22). The same idea in a milder form stands in 2 Maccabees, where the youngest brother asks God "in me and my brothers to stop the anger of the Almighty" (2 Maccabees 7:38). The question whether the sufferings of the faithful can atone for others is the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38.

Townshend noted that "the phrases fall with a familiar sound on our ears," but that the idea of atonement "is not more distinctively Christian than it is Jewish": the whole sacrificial system stood on substitution, Moses offered himself for the people (Exodus 32:32), and David asked that the punishment fall on him and his house and not on the people (2 Samuel 24:17). The servant of Isaiah 53 "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12). The New Testament says the same of Jesus: he came "to give his life as a ransom in place of many" (Mark 10:45), and "Christ too was offered up once to bear the sins of many" (Hebrews 9:28).

The word hilastērion is the sharpest question. Paul says, "God put him forward as the place of atonement, through faith, by his blood" (Romans 3:25), and 17:22 in Codex Sinaiticus uses the same word of the martyrs' death. In Sinaiticus it is a noun, "the hilastērion of their death"; in Alexandrinus, which Swete prints, an adjective, "their atoning death" (Swete's notes). Daniel Bailey (2000) argues that Sinaiticus is right here but that the two passages use different pictures: Paul's is the mercy seat of the Law, and 4 Maccabees uses the ordinary Greek sense, a gift offered to win a god's favor, so that "the common practice of paralleling Romans 3:25 and 4 Maccabees 17:22" should stop. See the variant note at 17:22 and the canon page below for how strong each link is.

The book's hope is the immortality of the soul. The brothers run "the road to immortality" (14:5); the mother was bearing her sons again, "this time into immortality" (16:13); "those who die for God's sake live to God, as Abraham, Isaac and Jacob do, and all the patriarchs" (16:25; compare 7:19); and at the end the sons with their mother are gathered "in the place of their fathers," and "From God they have received souls that are pure and immortal" (18:23). The wicked face eternal torment (9:9; 13:15; 18:5). Swete lists its belief in future punishment, eternal life for the righteous, and "the atonement for sin which is made by voluntary sacrifice." Townshend adds that "apparently there is no resurrection of the body," and traces the Alexandrian form of this hope to Plato.

Two textual questions touch this teaching. At 18:23 the first hands of Sinaiticus, and possibly of Alexandrinus, read "prize-winning" souls, later corrected to "immortal" (Swete's notes). And at 13:17 some later manuscripts add that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will receive the martyrs "into their bosoms"; Swete leaves the words out, and Townshend thought they might come from someone who knew Luke 16:23. Israel Abrahams (in the Jewish Encyclopedia, cited by Townshend) even wondered whether the sayings that the patriarchs "live to God" (7:19; 13:17; 16:25) were Christian additions; Townshend answered that nothing in them needs a Christian hand.

sections.h: The Holy Maccabees in the church
sections.b:
Jews did little with the book (Townshend), but Christians made its martyrs saints. The Orthodox Church keeps the seven Maccabee brothers, their mother Solomonia and their teacher Eleazar on 1 August, and names the brothers Abim, Antonius, Gurias, Eleazar, Eusebonus, Alimus and Marcellus (OCA). Townshend notes that they were "lauded by the Western as well as by the Eastern Church," in sermons of Augustine and Leo the Great and in the calendars of Carthage, of the Syrians and of the Arabians. Their shrine was at Antioch, "first Jewish and later Christian" (De Young).

The preachers knew 4 Maccabees itself. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his oration on the Maccabees (Oration 15), sends those who "love labour and learning" to "the book, which philosophizes about the Reason being supreme over the passions" (Townshend's translation), and insists that the martyrs "are not to be despised because they were before the Cross." John Chrysostom's sermons on them borrow the book's picture of an athletic contest, its comparison of the mother to the three young men in the furnace, and its image of Eleazar as a cliff against the waves (Townshend).

Later the names grew. A medieval Hebrew history, Josippon, calls the mother Hannah (Townshend). Erasmus, in his free Latin paraphrase (1517, enlarged 1524), calls her Solomona, gives the sons names, and reports that their relics were brought by Helena, mother of Constantine, to Byzantium, then to Milan, and in 1164 to Cologne (as Townshend quotes him).

The Plain English Translation is translated for this site from the Greek as printed by H. B. Swete in The Old Testament in Greek (volume 3, 1912), which follows Codex Alexandrinus (A) and gives the readings of Sinaiticus (ℵ) and Venetus (V) in its notes. Where the Plain English Translation departs from Swete's text, or where the codices differ in meaning, there is a variant note naming the witnesses (for example at 17:22 and 18:23). There is no King James, Vulgate or Douay-Rheims version of this book; Brenton's English of 1851 was used to check the sense. Its numbers differ from Swete's in chapters 7, 8, 10 and 11, so the site shows Swete's numbers.

Key words are kept the same in every chapter: ho eusebēs logismos is "godly reason," ta pathē "the passions," hypomonē "endurance," ho tyrannos "the tyrant." At 6:29 and 17:22, antipsychon is "a life in exchange" and katharsion "cleansing"; the Plain English Translation never uses "propitiation" or "expiation," and the notes explain both.

sections.h: Its place in Greek and other Bibles
sections.b:
The three great codices that have books of Maccabees all have this one: Sinaiticus, which has 4 Maccabees though not the second and third books (Swete), Alexandrinus and Venetus. De Young writes that "in later Greek manuscripts, 4 Maccabees is included in an appendix," while older ones make no such distinction and often place it near the end with Psalm 151 and the Prayer of Manasseh. The NRSV preface says that "4 Maccabees appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible." It was in Old Georgian Old Testaments, and for a time in the Romanian, where it bore the name of Josephus (De Young). It is not among the books of the Russian Synodal Bible as listed at azbyka.ru.

In the West it was hardly known. It is not in the Vulgate and so was "absent from the Apocrypha of the Roman Bible and from our own" (Townshend). Its Greek was first printed at Strassburg in 1526, and Erasmus made a free Latin paraphrase of it (Townshend). John Lloyd, an Oxford scholar, translated it "just two years after the defeat of the Great Armada" and mocked "certain Roman theologians" who wanted it received as canonical (Townshend).

spec.title: Claude's theory: Hebrews 12:1-2 as the contest of 4 Maccabees 17 with Jesus at its center
spec.body: In 17:10-17 the speaker pictures the martyrs' deaths as a divine contest: virtue sets the prize, endurance is tested, the world and the human race look on, and godliness crowns its athletes. They kept their eyes on God (eis theon aphorōntes, 17:10) and endured torture to death. Hebrews 12:1-2 uses the same picture: a great "cloud of witnesses" watching, a race run "with endurance," and "We fix our eyes on Jesus" (aphorōntes, the same verb, which Vincent's Word Studies notes in 17:10), who "endured a cross." My suggestion is that, whether or not the writer of Hebrews knew this book, a reader who knows it can see Hebrews taking the Jewish picture of the martyrs' contest and putting Jesus at its center: not one more athlete, but the one the runners look to, the "Founder and perfecter of faith" (Hebrews 12:2). I have not found this reading of Hebrews 12 in the scholarship I checked for this page, so it should be read as my own idea.

spec.title: Claude's theory: the mother measured against Abraham
spec.body: 4 Maccabees calls the mother one "who had a soul like Abraham's" (14:20) and has her recall that Abraham hurried to sacrifice Isaac and did not flinch at the knife (16:20). The rabbis' story of a mother and seven sons, told in a different setting and with different words, ends with her sending her youngest to Abraham with a message: "You bound one son to the altar, but I bound seven altars" (Bavli Gittin 57b). My suggestion is that both draw on a common Jewish way of telling martyr stories in which the binding of Isaac was the measure of a parent's faith, and the mother of seven was the one who surpassed it. The two texts do not depend on each other, which is what makes the shared comparison striking. I have not found this comparison in the scholarship I checked for this page, so it should be read as my own idea.

prompts:
On a high stone platform in a Greek city, a young king in a diadem sits enthroned among counselors, armed guards standing in a ring around him; before him an aged white-bearded priest in a plain robe stands upright, refusing a plate of meat a guard holds out; a crowd of captive men, women and children waits below.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.
The mother and her seven sons (14:11-15:32)

views: At the edge, not in the canon in the full sense. "4 Maccabees appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible" (the NRSV preface), and Fr. Stephen De Young calls it "a Biblical text that lies at the very edges of the Old Testament canon in the Orthodox Church": later Greek manuscripts put it in an appendix, older ones make no such distinction, and it is present in Old Georgian Old Testaments and was once in Romanian ones. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85) count "of the Maccabees, three" among the books "venerable and sacred," without saying which three. The same canon lists "two Epistles of Clemens" and the Constitutions of Clement among them, and has no Wisdom, Tobit or Baruch; the Council in Trullo (692), in its canon 2, ratified "the eighty-five canons" but in the same canon rejected the Constitutions, so canon 85 is not a church-wide list of the Old Testament. The Russian Synodal Bible, in its list of books at azbyka.ru, has three books of Maccabees and no fourth, and marks all three non-canonical. The NRSV preface, speaking of the churches and not of that printed list, says the books "up to and including 3 Maccabees are recognized as Deuterocanonical Scripture by the Greek and the Russian Churches." No Orthodox source opened for this page names 4 Maccabees as canonical. The martyrs themselves are saints of the Orthodox Church, kept on 1 August (OCA).

No, for the Coptic Orthodox Church, by the answer of its Diocese of the Southern United States to a reader who asked about 3 and 4 Maccabees: "There's no official statement, but since none of the early Church fathers spoke about these books, they are not included in the Canon." A Syriac version survives in many manuscripts (Townshend), but this page has no statement from the Syriac or Armenian churches themselves on the book's standing.

No. The church's list of its 46 Old Testament books names "I Maccabees" and "II and III Maccabees" and no fourth book. R. W. Cowley (1974), describing the canon of that church, says its three books of Maccabees (Mäqabeyan) "are not the same as any of the 4 LXX books of Maccabees"; so the books the list names are, on Cowley's account, other books, not the Greek 1-4 Maccabees.

No. The Council of Trent (1546) named "two books of the Machabees, the first and the second." The Catholic Encyclopedia (Bechtel) says that of four books of that name "the first and second only are regarded by the Church as canonical" and the fourth is apocryphal, with no "claim to canonicity." The book was never in the Vulgate (Townshend). The martyrs are honored in the West too, in the sermons of Augustine and Leo the Great (Townshend).

Not in Luther's Bible, not even among its Apocrypha. Luther headed the Apocrypha "Apocrypha. Das sind Bücher: so nicht der heiligen Schrift gleich gehalten: und doch nützlich und gut zu lesen sind" ("Apocrypha: these are books not held equal to Holy Scripture, and yet useful and good to read"), and took in Judith, Wisdom, Tobit, Sirach, Baruch, the first and second books of Maccabees, and the additions to Esther and Daniel (Martin Rösel, for the German Bible Society). That is Luther's choice for his Bible; this page has no statement of a Lutheran confession on 4 Maccabees.
No, and not among the books "the Church doth read for example of life and instruction of manners": the list of Article VI ends with the First and Second Books of Maccabees.

No. The Westminster Confession (1.3) says "The books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of Scripture," and 4 Maccabees was not even among the Apocrypha of the English Bible (Townshend). The Zurich Bible added 3 and 4 Esdras and 3 Maccabees to Luther's Apocrypha; Rösel does not name 4 Maccabees among them.

canon.summary: The NRSV preface says 4 Maccabees "appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible," and it was copied in Old Georgian and, for a time, Romanian Bibles (De Young), but no church source opened for this page counts it among its canonical books. The old lists disagree: the Apostolic Canons count three books of Maccabees without naming them, a Synopsis ascribed to Athanasius counts four outside its list, and the Claromontanus list names a first, second and fourth. It is not in the Russian Synodal, Coptic, Ethiopian, Catholic, Protestant or Jewish Bible. Its martyrs, Eleazar, the seven brothers and their mother, are saints of the Orthodox Church, kept on 1 August.
accepted_by: In an appendix, at the edge of the Old Testament. "4 Maccabees appears in an appendix to the Greek Bible" (NRSV preface). Fr. Stephen De Young writes that it "lies at the very edges of the Old Testament canon in the Orthodox Church": later Greek manuscripts put it in an appendix, older ones make no such distinction, and it is present in Old Georgian Old Testaments and was for a time in Romanian ones. The Apostolic Canons (canon 85) count "of the Maccabees, three" among the books "venerable and sacred," without naming the three, and list with them "two Epistles of Clemens" and the Constitutions of Clement, while leaving out Wisdom, Tobit and Baruch. The Council in Trullo (692, canon 2) ratified the eighty-five canons but rejected the Constitutions in the same canon, and it also sealed the canons of Carthage, which name "Macchabees, ij. books." The Russian Synodal Bible, in its list of books at azbyka.ru, has three books of Maccabees and no fourth, and marks the three "non-canonical" (неканоническая); the NRSV preface, speaking of the churches, says the Greek and Russian Churches recognize the books up to 3 Maccabees as Deuterocanonical Scripture. The Orthodox Church in America names "the Books of Maccabees" in its "longer canon" without a number. No Orthodox source opened for this page names 4 Maccabees as canonical.
Georgian Orthodox Church (read; no church statement found)
Present in Old Georgian Old Testaments (De Young). This page has no statement from the Georgian Church itself on the book's standing today.
Syriac churches (read; no church statement found)

A Syriac translation was made early: R. L. Bensly collated nine manuscripts of it, published by W. E. Barnes in 1895, and it was faithful enough to be used to correct the Greek, usually agreeing with Sinaiticus rather than Alexandrinus (Townshend). This page has no statement from the Syriac churches themselves on the book's standing.

Not canonical. Asked whether the Coptic Church ever made an official statement about 3 and 4 Maccabees, its Diocese of the Southern United States answered: "There's no official statement, but since none of the early Church fathers spoke about these books, they are not included in the Canon."
Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches

Not this book. The church's list of its 46 Old Testament books names "I Maccabees" and "II and III Maccabees," and no fourth. Cowley (1974) says the Ethiopian books of Maccabees (Mäqabeyan) "are not the same as any of the 4 LXX books of Maccabees," and gives their contents: a king of Media and Midian named Tsirutsaydan, a Benjaminite named Meqabis and his five sons, a king of Moab named Meqabis. That the books on the list are these Mäqabeyan, and not the Greek books, is the identification this page draws from Cowley.

Not Scripture. Trent (1546) named "two books of the Machabees, the first and the second." Bechtel, in the Catholic Encyclopedia, says the third and fourth are apocryphal and that neither has "any claim to canonicity"; Reid calls the book a "short philosophical treatise" that "was erroneously ascribed to Josephus." It was never in the Vulgate (Townshend).

Not in Luther's Bible. Its Apocrypha, headed "books not held equal to Holy Scripture, and yet useful and good to read" (der heiligen Schrift nicht gleich gehalten: und doch nützlich und gut zu lesen), have the first and second books of Maccabees only (Rösel, for the German Bible Society). This page has no statement of a Lutheran confession on the book.
Not Scripture, and not among the Apocrypha of Article VI, whose list ends with the First and Second Books of Maccabees.

Not Scripture. The Westminster Confession (1.3) holds that the books "commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the Canon of Scripture." 4 Maccabees was not even among the Apocrypha of the English Bible (Townshend). The Zurich Bible enlarged Luther's Apocrypha with 3 and 4 Esdras and 3 Maccabees (Rösel), not with this book.

Not Scripture. It is not in the Hebrew Bible, and "the direct influence of this book on Jewish literature does not seem to have been great" (Townshend), though the medieval Hebrew history Josippon shows traces of it. The rabbis told their own story of a mother and seven sons, set under a Roman emperor (Bavli Gittin 57b).

provenance.h: A Greek speech by a Jew of the Diaspora
provenance.b: The book was written in Greek, not translated. Its periods, its rhetorical figures and its new compound words have no Hebrew behind them, and Swete calls it nearer than any other book of the Greek Bible "to the models of Hellenic philosophy and rhetoric." Its writer was a Jew devoted to the law who "enlists the Stoic virtues in the cause of Jewish orthodoxy" (Townshend). He compares the martyrs' struggle to Greek games and wishes he could paint their story (17:7; 17:11-16), which Townshend thought easier to say in Alexandria than in Jerusalem.

The Temple and its service are spoken of as if still standing, and the speaker and hearers live in peace (14:9). From this Townshend dated it between 63 BC, when the Hasmonean high priesthood ended (he follows Grimm on the life tenure of Onias, 4:1), and AD 38, the persecution in Alexandria; Swete placed it in "the century before the fall of Jerusalem," and the Catholic Encyclopedia (Reid) before the fall too. Fr. Stephen De Young puts it at the end of the first century AD. For the place, Townshend and Swete chose Alexandria; De Young chose Antioch, where the martyrs' relics were kept in a shrine and where, by the OCA's account, the seven brothers were brought to trial.

The martyr stories come from 2 Maccabees 6:18-7:42 or from the longer history of Jason of Cyrene that 2 Maccabees abridges (Townshend; Swete). The writer reshapes them freely (see the section "How it retells 2 Maccabees"). The Bible stories behind the first part, Joseph and Potiphar's wife, the tenth commandment, Jacob's curse on Simeon and Levi, and David's thirst (2:1-3:18), are told as examples of reason ruling a passion, and the mother's last speech runs through the heroes and Scriptures her husband taught their sons (18:10-19).

The book is in Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD), which has it as Makkabaiōn d' without the second and third books, Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s-800s AD); Codex Vaticanus has no books of Maccabees (Swete; Townshend). Four leaves in a hand of the 800s AD, found in the binding of another manuscript, preserve parts of chapters 8 and 9 (Swete). It was also copied among the works of Josephus. Swete prints Alexandrinus with the other two in his notes. The Syriac version usually agrees with Sinaiticus (Townshend), and at 17:22 Bailey judges the Sinaiticus reading original and Alexandrinus "secondary."

A Syriac translation, which R. L. Bensly collated in nine manuscripts (Townshend). Eusebius and Jerome knew it as a work of Josephus. Gregory of Nazianzus and John Chrysostom drew on it in their sermons on the martyrs (Townshend). Erasmus made a very free Latin paraphrase, and the Greek was first printed at Strassburg in 1526 (Townshend).

provenance.h: What it builds on in the Hebrew Bible
provenance.b: The law of Moses is its center: the food laws of Leviticus 11 and Deuteronomy 14 (1:33-34; 5:2), the tenth commandment (2:5-6; Exodus 20:17), the laws on the poor, debts and enemies (2:8-14). Its examples are Joseph (2:2-3; Genesis 39), Jacob on Simeon and Levi (2:19-20; Genesis 49:7), David's thirst (3:6-18; 2 Samuel 23:13-17), Abraham's binding of Isaac (13:12; 16:20; Genesis 22), Daniel in the lions' den and the three young men in the furnace (13:9; 16:3, 21; Daniel 3; Daniel 6). The mother's last speech quotes or recalls Isaiah 43:2, Psalm 34:19, Proverbs 3:18, Ezekiel 37:3 and Deuteronomy 32:39 (18:14-19). Its picture of a righteous death that saves others stands near Isaiah 53.

rejected_why.h: It is not in the Jewish Bible
rejected_why.b: 4 Maccabees was written in Greek long after the Hebrew Scriptures were gathered, and it was never in the Hebrew Bible. It had little influence on later Jewish writing (Townshend). The Westminster Confession (1.3) holds that the books "commonly called Apocrypha" are "no part of the Canon of Scripture."

rejected_why.h: Almost no early list counts it
rejected_why.b:
The old lists of the books, as Swete prints them, treat the books of Maccabees in different ways, and only two can be read as naming a fourth book:

  • Origen (in Eusebius) ends his list by placing "the Maccabees" (ta Makkabaika) outside it, with no number.
  • Athanasius (Letter 39) and the Laodicene canons name no book of Maccabees at all.
  • The Apostolic Canons (canon 85) count "of the Maccabees, three" among the books "venerable and sacred," but do not say which three; Swete calls this an exception to the usual Eastern practice of leaving such books outside the canon.
  • The Stichometry of Nicephorus counts three books of Maccabees among the books it calls disputed and not read in church.
  • A Synopsis of Scripture ascribed to Athanasius adds four books of Maccabees to the books outside its list.
  • Carthage names "Macchabees, ij. books," and Trent "two books of the Machabees, the first and the second."
  • The Latin list in Codex Claromontanus names a first book of Maccabees, a second and a "fourth," with no third (Swete; bible-researcher.com, which prints the list from Westcott). Swete took the "fourth" to show that its maker knew of a third book. The list was copied into a Greek-Latin manuscript of Paul's letters of the 500s AD; when the list itself was made is uncertain.

So none of these lists makes 4 Maccabees canonical: the Greek list here that counts four puts them outside its canon, and the Latin list that names a fourth says nothing of its standing. A Coptic diocese gives the reason the book is not in that church's canon: "none of the early Church fathers spoke about these books."

rejected_why.h: It was never in the Latin Bible
rejected_why.b: The book is not in the Vulgate, so it was not in the Bible the Western church read, nor in the Apocrypha of the Reformers' Bibles, nor in Article VI (Townshend; Article VI). For Catholics the question was settled at Trent, which named two books of Maccabees; for Protestants it hardly arose. When John Lloyd of Oxford translated it in the late 1500s, he mocked "certain Roman theologians" who wanted it received as canonical on what they took to be Josephus's authority (Townshend).

The book calls Antiochus IV the son of Seleucus IV (4:15), raises Jason's price to 3,660 talents a year (4:17), and has Antiochus win all his wars by the martyrs' example (17:23-24), against what other sources say (Townshend). It hopes for immortal souls and never speaks of the resurrection of the body (18:23; Townshend), and it praises the mother's leap into the fire (17:1). For churches that do not hold it as Scripture, these are further reasons to read it as a human work: a powerful speech, not the Word of God.

The Orthodox do not reject the book; they keep it where their manuscripts and Bibles put it, at the edge. De Young explains that older Greek manuscripts made no distinction between it and the other books, and later ones placed it in an appendix; the church honors its martyrs and finds in its teaching on the passions a link to its own spiritual tradition. The Apostolic Canons, ratified at Trullo, count three books of Maccabees without naming them, and the Orthodox Church in America speaks of a "longer canon" without fixing the number of those books.

cited_in.b: "Others were tortured on the rack and would not take the release they were offered, so that they could win a better resurrection" (Hebrews 11:35). Meyer and the Expositor's Greek Testament both take the verse as an allusion to Eleazar and the seven brothers of 2 Maccabees 6-7 ("That Eleazar and the seven brethren (2 Maccabees 7) are alluded to is obvious," the Expositor's Greek Testament). 4 Maccabees comes in as an old illustration of the same scene: Meyer's commentary on the verse, explaining the instrument of torture, cites "Josephus, de Macc." (4 Maccabees under its old attribution) for the wheel, and the Expositor's Greek Testament says that "Josephus speaks of 'a wheel'" (compare 9:12). The word in Hebrews, etympanisthēsan, matches the tympanon of 2 Maccabees 6:19 and 6:28; 4 Maccabees has the wheel (trochos). The "better resurrection" of Hebrews matches the hope of 2 Maccabees 7:9, 14 rather than the immortal souls of 4 Maccabees (18:23), so if Hebrews has one book in mind it is most likely 2 Maccabees. The link to 4 Maccabees is to the same martyrs, not a quotation.

"Let us keep running the race that lies ahead of us, and keep at it with endurance. We fix our eyes on Jesus, the Founder and perfecter of faith" (Hebrews 12:1-2). Vincent's Word Studies, on "looking" (aphorōntes), cites 17:10, where the martyrs endured the tortures "fixing their eyes on God." The contest watched by the world, the endurance and the prize are also the picture of 17:11-16. A shared word and a shared picture, common in Greek moral writing; no one opened for this page argues that Hebrews quotes the book.

"God put him forward as the place of atonement, through faith, by his blood" (Romans 3:25). The Greek word is hilastērion, which 17:22 also uses of the martyrs' death in Codex Sinaiticus (Alexandrinus, which Swete prints, has the adjective, "atoning death"), with blood in both passages. Daniel Bailey writes of "the common practice of paralleling Romans 3:25 and 4 Maccabees 17:22," without naming its defenders in this summary, and argues against it: Paul means the mercy seat of the Law, the lid of the ark (Exodus 25:17-22; Leviticus 16:14-15; Hebrews 9:5), while 4 Maccabees uses the ordinary Greek sense, an offering that wins a god's favor. A debated background, not a citation; whether Paul knew the book cannot be shown.

Jesus says that God "is not God of dead people but of living ones, for to him all are alive" (Luke 20:38), and in the story of Lazarus the poor man is carried "to Abraham's embrace" (Luke 16:22). 4 Maccabees says that those who die for God "live to God" like the patriarchs (7:19; 16:25) and that Abraham, Isaac and Jacob will receive the martyrs (13:17). Here the question runs the other way: some later manuscripts add at 13:17 that the patriarchs will receive them "into their bosoms," which Swete leaves out and Townshend thought might be inserted by someone who knew Luke 16:23; Israel Abrahams (cited by Townshend) wondered whether the "live to God" sayings were Christian additions, and Townshend thought them Jewish. Townshend discusses only the Luke 16 link; setting Luke 20:38 beside 7:19 and 16:25 is this page's own comparison, not a commentator's. Shared Jewish hope, with a possible Christian touch in a few manuscripts.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to what Greek-speaking Jews believed in the first century AD, 4 Maccabees is of the first importance: it shows them joining Greek philosophy to the law of Moses, honoring martyrs, hoping for immortal souls with the patriarchs, and saying that a righteous death can cleanse the nation and stand "in exchange" for its sin. As a text it is well preserved in Greek, its original language, in three of the great codices and a faithful Syriac version, though the codices differ at a few key points (17:22; 18:23). As history it adds little to 2 Maccabees and has clear slips (4:15; 4:17; 17:23-24); it was never meant as a chronicle. Measured against the 66 books, it agrees on the one God, the goodness of the law and the faithfulness of the martyrs; it goes beyond them on the atoning power of the martyrs' blood and on reason's mastery; it leaves out the resurrection of the body; and in praising the mother's leap into the fire and in its confidence that trained reason can master every passion it sits uneasily beside the Bible's own teaching.

sections.h: 1. A witness to Jewish thought before and beside the New Testament: high
sections.b: Here the churches agree. The book shows a Jew of the Diaspora arguing that the law is the true philosophy (5:22-25), defining the virtues in Greek terms (1:18), and teaching that the soul is immortal (14:5-6; 18:23), that the wicked are punished forever (9:9; 13:15), that the patriarchs "live to God" (7:19; 16:25), and that the martyrs' deaths cleansed the homeland (1:11; 17:21-22). It also uses "faith" in a religious sense, "faith in God" (15:24; 16:22; 17:2), which Townshend thought belonged not to Greek thought but to the Hebrew mind. These are the ideas in the air when the New Testament was written, which is why scholars of Hebrews, Paul and the Gospels read it.

Well. The Greek is the original. It survives in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Venetus, in many later manuscripts and in the manuscripts of Josephus, with a Syriac version faithful enough to correct the Greek (Townshend). The codices differ at points that matter for doctrine: at 17:22 Sinaiticus has a noun, "the hilastērion of their death," where Alexandrinus has an adjective, "their atoning death"; at 18:23 the first hands read "prize-winning" souls where the corrected text has "immortal" (Swete's notes). The early printed editions came from a poor manuscript (Townshend). The attribution to Josephus is late and wrong (Townshend; the Catholic Encyclopedia).

What fits. The setting is real: Seleucus IV and Antiochus IV, the high priests Onias and Jason, a gymnasium in Jerusalem, the decree against the law (3:20-4:26), all of which 2 Maccabees 3-6 also tells.

What does not. Antiochus is called Seleucus's son, not his brother (4:15; Townshend); Apollonius, not Heliodorus, goes to the Temple treasury (4:1-14; 2 Maccabees 3:7); Jason's price is about ten times the 360 talents of 2 Maccabees (4:17; 2 Maccabees 4:8); and Antiochus is said to win all his wars by the martyrs' example (17:23-24). The tortures and speeches are the writer's art. The martyrdoms themselves come from 2 Maccabees, so their history is that book's, which the 2 Maccabees page weighs.

The answer of those who hold it in their Bibles. None of the Orthodox sources opened for this page rules on these questions. De Young reads the book as a melding of philosophical treatise and wisdom writing, not as history. A fair summary: a speech that uses a known story to prove a thesis, with historical slips that do not touch its purpose.

sections.h: 4. Agreement with the 66 books, point by point
sections.b:
• Agrees: the one God, "the God who truly is" (5:24), Creator of the world (5:25); the law of Moses as God's gift (2:23; 5:25); the food laws (5:2; Leviticus 11); faithfulness to death rather than idolatry, as with the three young men and Daniel (13:9; 16:21; Daniel 3:16-18); the righteous who suffer for others, as with the servant who "bore the sin of many" (Isaiah 53:12); the patriarchs alive to God, as Jesus taught: "to him all are alive" (7:19; Luke 20:38); and the tenth commandment, "You must not crave" (2:6; Romans 7:7).
  • Goes beyond: (a) the atoning death of martyrs: Eleazar asks that his blood be their cleansing and his soul taken as a life in exchange for them (6:28-29), and the speaker says their death saved Israel (17:22). The Old Testament has the idea in the servant of Isaiah 53 and in Moses' offer (Exodus 32:32), but never says it of martyrs; the New Testament gives this role to Christ alone, "offered up once to bear the sins of many" (Hebrews 9:28). The churches' answers on whether the sufferings of the faithful can share in it are on the card at 2 Maccabees 7:37-38. (b) Greek philosophy as the frame of the faith: the four virtues and reason's rule over the passions (1:18; 1:30).
  • Leaves out: the resurrection of the body, which 2 Maccabees 7:9 and 7:14, Daniel 12:2 and the New Testament teach; here the hope is the immortal soul (18:23). Also any Messiah.
  • May conflict: (a) reason's mastery: the book says that godly reason trained by the law can rule every passion (1:1; 2:21-23; 18:2). Paul says that the same tenth commandment showed him his craving and that the law could not free him from it (Romans 7:7-8), and that those who are Christ's "have crucified the flesh, with its passions and its desires" (Galatians 5:24) by the Spirit. How far the two can be reconciled is what the churches debate about grace and the law. (b) chosen death: the youngest brother throws himself into the fire (12:20) and the mother throws herself into it so that no one would touch her (17:1), and both are praised. In the Bible the faithful who die for God are put to death by others; how Jews and Christians judged such deaths is on the topic page on suicide.
  • Each church's view: the NRSV preface places it in an appendix to the Greek Bible, and the Orthodox honor its martyrs; for Catholics (Trent) and Protestants (Westminster 1.3) it is outside the canon.

how_to_read.b: If you are Eastern Orthodox, you may find 4 Maccabees in an appendix, at the edge of your Old Testament (De Young; the NRSV preface), though not in the Russian Synodal Bible, and you will find its martyrs in your calendar on 1 August (OCA). If you are Catholic or Protestant, it is not in your Bible and never was; read it as an ancient Jewish speech that your churches' preachers once loved. If you are Coptic or Ethiopian Orthodox, it is not in your church's canon.

Do not read it for the history; read it for the claim. Keep the question of 1:1 in mind and watch how each scene answers it. Ask whether you agree: can a mind trained by God's word rule fear and pain and desire? Then read Romans 7-8 and Galatians 5:16-25 beside it, where the answer is the Spirit.

Read 2 Maccabees 6:18-7:42 first, then chapters 5-18 here, and notice what the speaker adds, changes and leaves out: the priesthood of Eleazar, the long speeches, the mother's leap into the fire, and the hope of immortal souls in place of the raised body.

how_to_read.h: Read it beside Hebrews and the cross
how_to_read.b: Read 6:27-29 and 17:20-22 beside Isaiah 53, Mark 10:45, Romans 3:25 and Hebrews 9:28, and 17:11-16 beside Hebrews 11:35-12:2. The book helps you hear how first-century Jews spoke of a righteous death for others. Then ask what the New Testament says that this book does not: that one death was enough, once for all, and that the one who died rose again.
The book describes the tortures plainly and at length, as a proof of courage. Younger readers may want to read the speeches and skip the descriptions in chapters 6 and 9-12.
